title: When To Enforce A Consequence And When To Redo A Routine
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin answers a common question — when to give individual consequences during a botched routine versus sending the whole class back to redo it — by pointing to a natural pattern: off-track behavior during a routine is rarely evenly distributed, but tends to involve either a few students or most of the class. His rule is straightforward: if only a few students misbehave, enforce individual consequences; if most of the class is off track and the behavior is minor, send everyone back to redo the routine; if the class is disruptive and chaotic, stop and reteach the routine in detail as if for the first time. He warns that widespread minor misbehavior during a routine can be a sign the routine itself wasn't taught thoroughly enough, and treats major breakdowns as opportunities to raise standards. The piece closes with a concise summary of the decision rule for easy recall in the moment.
points: Off-track routine behavior tends to naturally fall into two patterns — a small number of students, or most of the class — rarely a middling range.
If only a few students misbehave during a routine, enforce individual consequences for those students specifically.
If most of the class is off track but the behavior is minor, send the whole class back to redo the routine rather than trying to track every individual.
If most of the class is disruptive and chaotic during a routine, stop and reteach it in full detail, since this signals the routine was not adequately taught.
Widespread minor misbehavior during a routine is often diagnostic — a sign the teacher needs to raise standards and re-teach with more precision.
quotes: It is one of the most common questions we get here at SCM: “When do I enforce a consequence and when do I redo a routine?
You see, when students fail to perform a routine as taught, in the vast majority of cases it’s either just a small number of students off track or it’s most of the class.
In other words, it’s very rarely in the mid-range of say, 6 to 15 students. So the rule is if it’s just a few, or less, then you enforce individual consequences.
Because, if most of your class is performing a routine incorrectly, then it’s a sign that you may need to reteach the routine in greater detail.
If, on the other hand, the class was disruptive and chaotic, then it's best to stop everything and reteach the routine as if it's the first time.

So the solution is to teach, model, and practice the routine in explicit detail. Raise the bar even higher than it was before, and teach with a passion that refuses to accept anything less than excellence.
